items.title: Most adult humans can't digest milk — and that's normal
items.claim: Babies make lactase to digest lactose in milk. In most of the world's adults, lactase production switches off after weaning. Adult milk-drinkers — common in Europeans and some African and Middle Eastern populations — carry a recently evolved mutation.

options.text: Adult lactose intolerance is ancestral; lactase persistence is a derived trait that arose in populations that domesticated dairy animals in the last 10,000 years

items.reveal:
Roughly 65 percent of adult humans globally show reduced lactase production after weaning. Lactase persistence is most common in northern Europeans (around 90 percent), some West African pastoralist groups, and some Middle Eastern populations.

Different regulatory mutations independently produced this trait in different lineages — convergent evolution. The European variant (a single nucleotide change near the LCT gene, called T-13910) is dated to about 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, coinciding with cattle domestication.

Dairy farming and lactase persistence appear to have co-evolved: ancient DNA shows farmers drank milk before persistence was common, suggesting cultural use (fermented dairy, lower lactose) preceded biological adaptation. As populations relied more on milk, the persistence allele was strongly selected.
items.why: European diets are taken as a baseline; lactose intolerance is treated as a disorder. Globally, lactose intolerance IS the baseline — milk drinking adults are the rare ones.

items.title: Plants and oceans cycle far more CO2 than humans release — yet we still drive the trend
items.claim: Humans emit ~10 gigatonnes of carbon per year. Natural fluxes (photosynthesis ~120 Gt, ocean exchange ~80 Gt, respiration ~120 Gt) dwarf this. Yet atmospheric CO2 keeps rising. The natural fluxes are roughly balanced — human emissions are a small but unmatched addition.
items.prompt: Why does a small flux dominate the trend?

options.text: The large natural fluxes are bidirectional and roughly balanced; the small human flux is NET addition. Imagine a bath whose inflow exactly equals outflow — a slow added trickle raises the water level whether the main flow is large or not
Plants absorb only certain types of CO2

items.reveal_title: Flux vs reservoir vs net change
items.reveal:
Reservoirs (rough sizes in gigatonnes of carbon):
Atmosphere: ~880 (and rising)
Oceans: ~38,000 (most as dissolved bicarbonate, slow exchange with deep ocean)
Soils: ~1,500-2,400
Vegetation: ~450-650
Fossil fuels: ~4,000+ (decreasing as we burn them)

Fluxes (Gt C per year):
Photosynthesis: ~120 (atmosphere to land)
Land respiration: ~120 (back to atmosphere)
Ocean uptake: ~80 (atmosphere to ocean)
Ocean release: ~78 (ocean to atmosphere)
Fossil emissions: ~10 (geological store to atmosphere)
Land-use change: ~1-2 net (mostly deforestation)

The natural fluxes are within ~1% of balance. The fossil flux is unbalanced — it's NET addition with no matching natural removal at the same scale. About half is absorbed by oceans and land 'sinks'; half stays airborne. Atmospheric CO2 rises ~2.5 ppm/year.

Residence time vs adjustment time: an individual CO2 molecule exchanges with the ocean in years. But removing the EXCESS takes much longer (hundreds to thousands of years for the surface ocean, ~100,000 years for full geological recovery).
items.why: The 'humans only emit 4% of CO2 turnover' argument confuses flux with net change. A small net addition into a near-balanced cycle is what matters, and it accumulates.

items.title: Each of your sperm/eggs is one of 2 to the 23rd power possibilities
items.claim: Meiosis shuffles 23 chromosome pairs into 23 gametes. From you alone, ignoring recombination, that's 8.4 million possible combinations. Add crossing over and the count is effectively infinite. Why is sexual reproduction so expensive to maintain?
items.prompt: Why has sex (rather than cloning) persisted in almost all eukaryotes?

options.text: Sex is uniformly better than cloning

Sex generates genetic variation that helps populations adapt to changing environments (the Red Queen hypothesis: ongoing host-parasite arms races favour variability); also recombination weeds out accumulated harmful mutations more efficiently than clonal lineages can
Sex is necessary for cell division

items.reveal_title: The twofold cost and the Red Queen
items.reveal:
A sexually reproducing female passes 50 percent of her genes to each offspring. An asexual female passes 100 percent. Asexual lineages should outcompete sexual ones by a factor of two each generation. They mostly don't.

Leading explanations:
- Red Queen (Hamilton, Van Valen): parasites and pathogens evolve to attack common host genotypes; sexual reproduction keeps host genotypes shifting so parasites can't catch up.
- Muller's ratchet: asexual lineages accumulate harmful mutations and cannot purge them efficiently. Recombination lets harmful mutations be separated from beneficial ones.
- Fisher-Muller: sex can combine beneficial mutations from different lineages.

Observationally, almost all asexual lineages are evolutionarily young, suggesting they accumulate problems and go extinct.
items.why: Sex's costs are enormous and obvious; its benefits are subtle and long-term. Evolution favours it anyway, and the reasons are still debated.
